claim: A meta-analysis can be part of a systematic review, but a systematic review can exist without one; they are not synonyms.
limitations: Abstract does not state the distinction verbatim; the distinction is standard (Cochrane Handbook ch.1) but the Handbook was not read this session.

claim: Scoping reviews are appropriate to identify knowledge gaps, scope a body of literature, clarify concepts or investigate research conduct, and may precede a systematic review.
limitations: Single group's (JBI) guidance; other groups' views on scope/appraisal differ.

claim: PRISMA-ScR is the reporting guideline for scoping reviews (20 essential items + 2 optional).
limitations: Check for newer scoping-review reporting updates before use.

claim: SWiM is a reporting guideline for synthesis without meta-analysis of effect estimates in reviews of interventions (nine items).
limitations: Scope limited to intervention reviews with quantitative data.

claim: In a pilot randomised study of 31 clinicians, PICO-based search templates showed a higher-precision trend but no statistically significant difference versus standard PubMed searching.
limitations: Small pilot; evaluates search interfaces, not question quality.

claim: I-squared depends on study precision and can approach 100% as studies get larger even when tau-squared is unchanged; tau-squared rather than I-squared should guide judgments of clinical relevance of heterogeneity.
limitations: Argument concerns using I2 to decide on pooling; does not say I2 is useless.

claim: H and I-squared (Q-based) are proposed as measures of heterogeneity impact independent of the number of studies and the effect metric, to be reported in preference to the Q test.
limitations: Later literature (Rucker 2008) cautions about I2's dependence on precision.

claim: Fixed-effect and random-effects models embody different assumptions and are not interchangeable; model choice should reflect the goals/context of the analysis.
limitations: Tutorial/position paper by authors of a widely used textbook; other methodologists hold different defaults.

claim: Langan et al. (2019) recommended REML for estimating the heterogeneity variance, found DerSimonian-Laird negatively biased with small studies and rare binary outcomes, and Paule-Mandel positively biased with large differences in study size; they caution tau-squared is unreliable with few studies.
limitations: Simulation scenarios are finite; the recommendation is conditional on them. MetaLab therefore presents REML as a reasonable default, not as universally optimal.

claim: Veroniki et al. (2016) found Paule-Mandel generally, and REML for continuous data, better alternatives to DerSimonian-Laird; Q-profile is recommended for tau-squared confidence intervals.
limitations: Qualitative evaluation + expert consensus, as the abstract itself states.

claim: The Hartung-Knapp(-Sidik-Jonkman) approach keeps nominal coverage better than usual fixed/random-effects tests in simulations and is robust to the tau-squared estimator.
limitations: Hartung & Knapp 2001 studied binary outcomes; the robustness-to-estimator statement comes from Langan 2019 (C009). Truncation (q*<1) handling varies between software.

claim: A prediction interval describes the range of true effects in a new study and should accompany random-effects results.
limitations: Bibliographic record verified (title: 'Interpretation of random effects meta-analyses') but content NOT examined; claim rests on standard methodological practice.

claim: The t(k-2) prediction interval for k>=3 studies (Riley 2011) differs from metafor's default z-based interval; both are implemented and benchmarked.
limitations: The t(k-2) formula itself is checked only against our own computation of it, not against an independent implementation.

claim: The exact small-sample correction J = Gamma(df/2)/(sqrt(df/2)Gamma((df-1)/2)) differs by ~1% from 1-3/(4df-1) at df=2.
limitations: Original paper not read; exact form confirmed by metafor agreement to 1e-9.

claim: Several lifespan-intervention meta-analyses already exist (e.g., DR in rodents, rapamycin in mice, rapamycin vs metformin in vertebrates), so DR/rapamycin lifespan is a crowded area.
limitations: One database; reviews' scope/overlap not read; this is a signal, not a novelty determination.

claim: PRESS is a guideline for peer review of electronic search strategies (2015 guideline statement).
limitations: Only the title was examined; the content/checklist items were not read.

claim: PRISMA-S is an extension to PRISMA for reporting literature searches in systematic reviews.
limitations: Items of the checklist not examined.

claim: Free-text sentences are translated by PubMed with automatic term mapping into ANDed concepts, which can yield 0 results (and 'STEM' was mapped to plant stems/electron microscopy).
limitations: Observed behaviour on one date; PubMed's algorithm can change.

claim: Data-extraction and reporting errors were found with high prevalence but low impact in Cochrane systematic reviews.
limitations: Only the title was examined; the magnitude and definition of 'impact' were not read.

claim: A methodological review of the frequency of data-extraction errors and of methods to increase extraction quality exists (Mathes 2017).
limitations: Findings (error rates, effectiveness of double extraction) not read; lesson avoids quoting rates.

claim: SYRCLE's risk-of-bias tool for animal studies exists (Hooijmans 2014).
limitations: Existence only.

claim: SYRCLE's tool has ten items (sequence generation, baseline characteristics, allocation concealment, random housing, blinding of caregivers/investigators, random outcome assessment, blinding of outcome assessor, incomplete outcome data, selective outcome reporting, other).
limitations: Item list recalled from author knowledge; check against the paper/official guidance.

claim: Cochrane RoB 2 has five domains (randomisation process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, selection of the reported result).
limitations: Recalled; check official RoB 2 guidance (version/date).

claim: ROBINS-I has seven bias domains from confounding to selection of the reported result.
limitations: Recalled; check official guidance.

claim: QUADAS-2 has four domains: patient selection, index test, reference standard, flow and timing.
limitations: Recalled; check the paper.

claim: The log response ratio variance sd1^2/(n1 m1^2)+sd2^2/(n2 m2^2) (Hedges et al. 1999) matches metafor's ROM implementation.
limitations: Original paper not read; agreement with metafor to 1e-7.

claim: Q-based I2 (Higgins & Thompson) and tau2-based I2 (as printed by metafor) are both in use; they differ slightly (BCG 92.1% vs 92.2%).
limitations: metafor's definition verified from its output/behaviour, not from documentation text.

claim: Methods exist to estimate the sample mean and SD from the median, range and/or IQR (Wan 2014); they rely on distributional assumptions.
limitations: Existence supported by title; the assumption/bias caveats stated in the lesson are general knowledge, not read from the paper.

claim: Evidence-based research initiatives argue new studies should be justified by existing systematic reviews of the evidence.
limitations: Content not read (Crossref has no abstract); lesson cites it only as further reading.

claim: PRISMA-P provides a checklist of items to report in a systematic review protocol.
limitations: Items not read.

claim: Analyses of registered reviews report the time and number of workers needed for medical systematic reviews (Borah 2017); a similar analysis exists for environmental reviews (Haddaway & Westgate 2018).
limitations: Magnitudes not read; lesson gives orders of magnitude only.

claim: Studies exist on optimal database combinations for systematic review searches (Bramer 2017) and on the suitability of academic search systems (Gusenbauer & Haddaway 2020).
limitations: Findings not read; the lesson draws only practical advice (use >=2-3 subject databases) from general practice.

claim: At least two or three subject-appropriate databases should be searched and Google Scholar treated as a supplement.
limitations: General methods practice; not verified against the cited papers' content.

claim: A stepwise EndNote de-duplication procedure with manual checks exists (Bramer et al. 2016).
limitations: Details not read.

claim: Cohen's kappa corrects observed agreement for chance and is prevalence-dependent; Landis & Koch benchmarks are conventions.
limitations: Standard statistics; McHugh 2012 abstract not read here. Formula verified by hand-computed example in tests.

claim: A methodological review compared single versus conventional double screening for study selection (Waffenschmidt 2019).
limitations: Result (single screening can miss studies) is the lesson author's summary, not read in the paper.

claim: Intercoder reliability and validity of WebPlotDigitizer in extracting graphed data have been evaluated (Drevon 2016).
limitations: Findings not read.

claim: robvis is an R package and Shiny app for visualising risk-of-bias assessments.
limitations: Features beyond title not examined.

claim: Continuity corrections in sparse-data meta-analysis have drawbacks and alternatives exist (Sweeting 2004; Bradburn 2007).
limitations: Titles indicate topic ('What to add to nothing?'; 'Much ado about nothing'); conclusions not read.

claim: Exact two-sided p-value to SE conversion SE=|estimate|/z is valid only for the same estimate's Wald/t test.
limitations: Identity checked in tests; no external source cited for the caveats.
